blocks.prompt: 11. Let \(g: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) be given by \(g(x) = x^{3}\ \ 3x\) [the sign between the terms is missing in print; read as \(x^{3} - 3x\)]. Determine if \(g(x)\) is injective and/or surjective.
blocks.explanation:
Injective = one-to-one; surjective = onto. Test both for \(g(x) = x^3 - 3x\).
To show "not injective", one counter-example (two inputs, same output) is enough.
Plan: a small table of values for injectivity; for surjectivity use the behaviour of a cubic at both ends.
steps:
Given: \(g: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\), \(g(x) = x^3 - 3x\).
To find: whether \(g\) is injective and whether it is surjective.
Method: Table of values to find equal outputs; then show \(x^3 - 3x = y\) has a real solution for every real \(y\).

Table of values
\[g(-2) = -8 + 6 = -2\]
\[g(-1) = -1 + 3 = 2\]
\[g(0) = 0,\quad g(1) = -2,\quad g(2) = 2\]
Why: Small whole numbers are quick to compute and show the pattern.

Not injective
\[g(1) = g(-2) = -2,\quad 1 \ne -2\]
Why: Two different inputs give the same output. (Also \(g(0) = g(\sqrt{3}) = 0\), since \(x^3 - 3x = x(x^2 - 3)\).)

Surjective
\[x \to \infty:\; x^3 - 3x \to \infty\]
\[x \to -\infty:\; x^3 - 3x \to -\infty\]
Why: For large \(|x|\) the \(x^3\) term dominates. The graph is one unbroken curve going from \(-\infty\) up to \(\infty\), so it crosses every horizontal line \(y = c\) at least once: \(x^3 - 3x = c\) (a cubic with real coefficients) always has a real root.

Check with an example
\[c = 18:\; x = 3,\ 27 - 9 = 18 \;\checkmark\]
Why: A chosen output is reached. The graph shows the line \(y = -2\) meeting the curve twice (not injective) while every horizontal line meets it at least once (surjective).
blocks.final_answer: \(g(x) = x^3 - 3x\) is surjective (onto) but not injective (e.g. \(g(1) = g(-2) = -2\)); so it is not bijective.

It crosses the x-axis at minus root 3, 0 and root 3. A dashed horizontal line y = -2 touches the curve at x = 1 and meets it again at x = -2, showing two inputs with the same output. blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints \(g(x) = x^{3}\ \ 3x\) with the sign between the terms missing. It should be \(g(x) = x^{3} - 3x\): the key's answer "g(x) is surjective" (and not injective) fits only this. With a plus sign, \(x^{3} + 3x\) would always increase and be both injective and surjective. (The key prints this answer on Question 9's line.)
